doc.title: Jimmy Witherspoon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, FL, April 12, 1996

title: White disc jockeys, radio and early rock and roll
summary: He discusses white disc jockeys playing rhythm and blues, Alan Freed, Hunter Hancock, and Sam Phillips discovering Elvis.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Yes. See I can’t understand the system. During that time there was mostly white disc jockeys, but they had black shows. You had Nashville, in Tennessee, why you could get all over America. But it was white disc jockeys, you had, Atlanta, Georgia, white disc jockeys were the top jockeys. You have white jockeys today who won’t play black music, I mean black blues. It’s kind of funny, isn’t it?
It’s funny and it’s still going on because tonight, your audience, you know—
They know what it is and I can’t understand it either.
The man who ran this record shop used to be from Nashville, Tennessee. Nothing but rhythm & blues.
Well that’s the foundation for rock & roll, too.
I know it. What’s his name was in Cleveland.
Alan Freed. Chess set him up. So you had Hunter Hancock was in Los Angeles. So you had big white disc jockeys. And I mean they were selling records.
And then you had Sam Phillips, making recordings in Memphis.
And recording some great black artists, but he didn’t really make his money until he found Elvis, who was singing black music.
